en.anatomyBody: In www.example.com, .com is the top-level domain (TLD). “example” is the name registered directly under it. “www” is an optional label added in front of that registered name.
en.rootBody: The invisible top of the DNS hierarchy.
en.secondBody: The name immediately to the left of the TLD, for example example.com.
en.hostBody: An optional label added in front of the registered name. In www.example.com, “www” can identify a specific site or service; it is not part of the TLD.
en.whoSub: The Internet has no single “owner”. It works through distinct roles, contracts and technical coordination.
en.roleIcannBody: Coordinates policies and contracts for generic top-level domains through a global multistakeholder model.
en.roleIanaBody: Acts as Root Zone Manager: PTI receives and validates TLD change requests and manages the authoritative delegation data for the DNS root.
en.roleRegistryBody: Operates a TLD and its authoritative registry database. gTLD operators work under ICANN registry agreements; ccTLD governance arrangements differ.
en.roleRspBody: Provides critical technical registry services such as DNS and registration infrastructure for the registry operator.
en.roleRegistrarBody: For gTLDs, an ICANN-accredited registrar provides the direct registration channel to registrants. ccTLDs use their own registry and registrar models.
en.roleRegistrantBody: The person or organization that registers and uses a domain name under the TLD.
en.birthTitle: How a new TLD is born
en.birthSub: The 2026 process is not “apply and receive”. It is a staged public process.
en.step1b: Applicant files the application and pays the required fee.
en.step2b: ICANN publishes public application data and identifies identical-string contention.
en.step3b: Community input, formal objections and relevant government advice can enter the process.
en.step4b: String, applicant, operational, financial and technical components are evaluated.
en.step5b: If multiple applicants seek the same or confusingly similar string, the contention must be resolved.
en.step6b: A successful applicant signs the Base Registry Agreement with ICANN.
en.step7b: After onboarding and technical checks, IANA/PTI processes the delegation request and the Root Zone Maintainer implements the validated change in the DNS root.
en.step8b: Only then can the registry move toward actually using and allocating names under the TLD.

en.secondGen: A second generation of city TLDs?
en.secondGenBody: The first wave was largely about identity, locality and registration. A 2026 city namespace can also be designed around trusted public services, verifiable identity, machine-readable governance and interaction with AI agents. That is an editorial hypothesis, not an ICANN classification.

en.tl1984Body: RFC 920 described .arpa as the initial, transitional top-level domain for the ARPA-Internet while the DNS was being introduced. It was supposed to disappear; instead it survived and today serves Internet infrastructure.
en.tl1985Body: In January 1985, .com, .edu, .gov, .mil, .net and .org joined .arpa in the root. On 15 March, symbolics.com became the first registered .com domain.
en.tl1999Body: The .berlin concept is traced back to 1999.
en.tl2012Body: 1,930 applications for 1,409 distinct strings, including 66 geographic applications.
en.tl2014Body: .berlin opens to the public; .nyc and .paris are delegated.
en.tl2026Body: 1,616 paid applications proceed. Reveal Day: 7 October 2026. .lugano enters the picture.
en.cNyc: A city-TLD application already existed in 2000.
en.cKids: Several applicants wanted a dedicated namespace for children.
en.cHealth: The World Health Organization proposed a dedicated health namespace.
en.cUnion: The international trade-union movement applied for .union.
en.cWap: A pure fossil from the WAP/mobile-web era.
en.cGeo: A geographic namespace concept well before the 2012 city wave.
en.cMuseum: One of the seven selected proof-of-concept TLDs.
en.cName: Personal identity imagined directly in the namespace.
en.cPost: Public-service infrastructure; the postal sector returned with .post in 2004.
en.sKids: Multiple applicants proposed .kids in 2000; one application also paired it with .xxx.
en.iKids: The early Web was already asking whether children needed a distinct, governed space rather than merely filtered content.
en.iHealth: Long before today’s arguments about online misinformation, public-health actors were already thinking about trust at the naming layer.
en.sUnion: The International Confederation of Free Trade Unions applied for .union.
en.iUnion: Industrial-era collective institutions were actively looking for a native place in the new digital public sphere.
en.sNyc: A .nyc application existed in 2000 and was later withdrawn.
en.iNyc: The desire for city identity online appeared before ICANN had a mature framework for city TLDs.
en.sSucks: Name.Space proposed .sucks in 2000; a .sucks gTLD was eventually delegated in 2015.
en.iSucks: A provocative idea moved from fringe proposal to production infrastructure. The boundary of what “belongs” in the root expanded dramatically.
en.sWar: .war appeared in the huge Name.Space bundle of proposed strings.
en.iWar: The proposal treated the DNS almost as a taxonomy of human life, including its darkest categories.
en.iSoup: The early expansion debate sometimes assumed that almost any semantic category could deserve a top-level namespace.
en.iMagic: Early Internet naming still carried a distinctly utopian belief that broad concepts could become self-contained digital places.
en.sMobi: .mobi was proposed in the 2004 sponsored round and later delegated.
en.iMobi: Before responsive design and smartphones normalized one Web, mobile looked different enough to deserve its own namespace.
en.sMail: .mail was proposed as a sponsored namespace but was not delegated.
en.iMail: Spam and trust were already serious enough problems that some actors tried to solve them at the naming layer.
en.sCat: .cat was created for the Catalan linguistic and cultural community.
en.iCat: A TLD did not need to map neatly onto a sovereign state: culture and language could also become infrastructure.
en.sPost: .post came from the Universal Postal Union.
en.iPost: One of the oldest global communications infrastructures tried to map itself into the architecture of the Internet.
en.sXxx: .xxx became one of the most contentious sponsored-TLD stories.
en.iXxx: Naming decisions are not merely technical; they can become proxies for wider political, cultural and regulatory conflicts.
en.iGuru: The 2010s turned expertise itself into a marketable online identity.
en.iNinja: The playful job-title vocabulary of startup and developer culture reached the DNS root.
en.iRich: Status and exclusivity became explicit identity categories that could be bought and signalled online.
en.iDating: As platforms specialized, intimate life also became a commercial vertical in the namespace.
en.sGop: .gop was delegated to a US political organization.
en.iGop: Political identity itself became a branded namespace, showing how far the 2012 round pushed specialization.
en.iLgbt: Community and identity could be represented directly at the top level of the naming system.
en.iBible: Faith communities joined brands, places and industries in claiming explicit space in the root.
en.iBeer: Products were no longer only things sold online; they became lifestyle categories with their own namespaces.
en.iPizza: Everyday consumption became part of the DNS vocabulary, from sectors and brands down to food culture.
en.iWtf: Internet slang itself became infrastructure, perhaps the most concise proof that the namespace had become culturally mainstream.
en.iFail: Even failure became a viable semantic category in the DNS root. The namespace had moved far beyond institutional labels.

en.beyondSub: Some namespaces went far beyond naming. They added eligibility, verification, security rules, public-interest governance or shared digital services.
en.maturityTitle: From a name to a trust layer
en.maturitySub: The interesting shift is not the number of domains. It is how much meaning and verification the namespace can carry.
en.m4b: Technical requirements become part of the namespace.
en.m5b: The TLD becomes a platform for common services.
en.casePostTitle: A TLD with a service layer
en.casePostBody: The UPU vets registrants, mandates a cybersecurity framework and operates trust.post, a Shared Services Platform for the postal and logistics sector.
en.caseCatTitle: A domain that funds a digital commons
en.caseCatBody: The .cat registry reinvests its revenues in digital rights, tools and projects for the Catalan-speaking community, describing the wider mission as civic infrastructure.
en.caseBankBody: Resolving .bank and .insurance domains must implement requirements such as DNSSEC, TLS and email authentication. The suffix is designed to signal a higher-trust environment.
en.caseGovTitle: The suffix itself is an institutional credential
en.caseGovBody: Only verified U.S. government organizations can register .gov. CISA verifies eligibility and the identity of requesters before approval.
en.casePharmacyBody: A registrant must first demonstrate compliance with NABP standards and receive accreditation. The domain is connected to an external qualification process.
en.caseEcoTitle: Activation requires a profile and a pledge
en.caseEcoBody: A .eco registration remains on hold until the registrant affirms eligibility, completes an Eco Profile and makes a public environmental commitment.
en.caseSwissTitle: A namespace reserved for a defined community
en.caseSwissBody: .swiss is restricted to the Swiss community and applies eligibility rules linking the registrant and the requested name to Switzerland.
en.geoTitle: The geography of power in the DNS
en.geoSub: Rules, registry contracts, technical infrastructure and applicant demand have different geographies. Explore each layer separately to understand where decisions and capabilities concentrate.
en.geoPlacesNote: Curated examples of city and territorial TLDs. This layer shows what a namespace represents, not a complete census and not where its technical backend is located.
en.geoGovernanceNote: Selected organizational locations for ICANN, PTI/IANA and the Root Zone Maintainer. ICANN policy is a global multistakeholder process; PTI validates root changes and Verisign implements them. Headquarters are not a map of where root service or Internet traffic physically runs.
en.geoRspNote: Evaluated RSP organizations by ICANN region as of 31 August 2026: Europe 16, Asia-Pacific 7, North America 6, Africa 0, Latin America & Caribbean 0. This is the geography of pre-evaluated technical supply. Applicants’ selected RSPs are not publicly posted in the 2026 application data (Question 176), so this is not applicant market share.
en.registryGeoBody: The useful answer has three layers: the place a TLD represents, the legal home of its registry operator, and the distributed technical backend. IANA records the TLD manager for every delegation. A full manager-country aggregation will be added with the 2026 dataset rather than inferred from brand names or server locations.
en.powerBody: Policy, root-zone management, maintenance, registry operations and technical backends are different roles. Mapping them separately reveals concentration without pretending that one organization “owns the Internet”.
en.rootStat3: 2,045 operational root-server instances as of 12 Sep 2026
en.mapHint: Select a layer to explore the map. Hover or tap a marker for context.
en.nodeLA: ICANN headquarters and Public Technical Identifiers (IANA functions).
en.nodeReston: Verisign headquarters; Verisign performs Root Zone Maintainer services.
en.luganoTitle: .lugano — from a name to a trust layer
en.luganoSub: A vision for what the namespace could become if the application succeeds. This is direction, not an announcement of services already implemented.
en.luganoLead: The ambition is not simply to put Lugano after a dot. It is to create a public-interest namespace in which trust can become visible, governable and eventually machine-readable.
en.lugPillar1b: Public responsibilities, access criteria and review procedures should be identifiable in the published rules.
en.lugPillar2b: Different classes of users or services could carry explicit eligibility and accountability rules.
en.lugPillar3b: Minimum technical requirements and open interfaces can make trust operational rather than merely symbolic.
en.lugPillar4b: In the longer term, software and AI agents could verify who they are interacting with, what a service is allowed to do and which rules apply.
en.lugRoadmapSub: Each step would require its own governance, legal and technical decisions after a successful ICANN process.
en.lugStage1b: Registry policies, reserved names, institutional domains, abuse handling and operational continuity.
en.lugStage2b: Qualified organizations, services and local actors with clear conditions of use and transparent responsibilities.
en.lugStage3b: Shared technical components, metadata and interoperable services that reduce friction for the local ecosystem.
en.lugStage4b: Machine-readable identity, delegation and service discovery so intelligent systems can evaluate trust as well as humans do.
en.luganoGuard: Nothing in this section implies that ICANN has assigned .lugano or that these services already exist. It describes a possible design direction, subject to the application outcome and future decisions by the City.
en.geoSourceLine: Method: policy, root coordination, contracts, technical backend and demand are separate layers. Geographic concentration is evidence of asymmetry, not proof that one place or company “controls the Internet”.
en.beyondQuote: Some of the clearest examples show that a TLD can encode more than a name: eligibility, identity, security, community rules and shared services.
en.legendText: verified information · interpretation of the data · future scenario
en.delegationCaveat: ICANN reports 1,241 delegations from the 2012 round; this total is not adjusted for TLDs later terminated or removed from the root zone.
en.roundAtGlanceSub: Four openings, radically different scales. Values are application counts, not the number of TLDs ultimately delegated.

en.powerStackTitle: Power is a stack, not a dot on a map
en.powerStackSub: Five layers matter, and they describe different things. Collapsing them into one “center of the Internet” would be neat, dramatic and wrong.
en.powerRulesBody: ICANN’s global multistakeholder process develops policy; ICANN org implements the contractual and program framework for gTLDs.
en.powerRootBody: PTI validates root-zone change requests; Verisign implements validated changes as Root Zone Maintainer. Root serving itself is distributed among independent operators worldwide.
en.powerContractsBody: Each gTLD registry operator holds contractual responsibility for its namespace. Some operators hold large portfolios of registry agreements.
en.powerBackendBody: Registry Service Providers supply registry, DNS and DNSSEC infrastructure across many TLDs. Technical concentration can differ sharply from ownership.
en.powerDemandBody: Applicants decide which strings are worth pursuing. Their public business locations reveal where commercial, civic and institutional demand originates.
en.geoMapSub: Switch layers to see institutional coordination, evaluated technical supply and applicant demand. They overlap, but they are not the same kind of power.
en.applicantRegion2026Note: After Reveal Day, this distribution will be derived from applicants’ public primary business locations in the official 2026 dataset. It will map applicant organizations, not users, DNS infrastructure or the geography of final economic activity.
en.demand2012Sub: ICANN recorded 1,930 applications from 60 countries and territories. North America and Europe together accounted for 82.2% of them.
en.rspSupplySub: By August 2026, 29 organizations had cleared at least one RSP evaluation. Europe alone accounted for 16, or 55.2%.
en.demand2026Sub: After Reveal Day this view will be derived from public primary business locations in the official 2026 dataset. It will describe applicant demand, not infrastructure geography.
en.topCountries2026Sub: After Reveal Day, this ranking will be derived from applicants’ public primary business locations in the official 2026 dataset.
en.identityTitle: Who built the broadest TLD portfolio? Donuts → Identity Digital
en.identitySub: Donuts filed 307 applications through subsidiaries in 2012. The business expanded through acquisitions and now operates as Identity Digital. A member biography on the ICANN SSAC website describes it as the world’s largest TLD registry operator; this is not an independently measured market-share ranking.
en.identityPortfolio: TLDs in Identity Digital’s current portfolio
en.identityManaged: TLDs Identity Digital says it manages technically
en.identityPortfolioClaim: Identity Digital describes a portfolio of nearly 300 TLDs. It also says it technically manages 460+ gTLDs, ccTLDs and dotBrands as a Registry Services Provider. Those are different measures: portfolio ownership / operation is not the same as technical backend management.
en.identityReadingBody: Registry operations carry substantial fixed costs in infrastructure, security, compliance and registrar distribution. A broad portfolio lets an operator reuse the same backend and sales channels, spread risk across niche strings and grow further through acquisitions. Donuts explicitly cited economies of scale as a core reason for applying for hundreds of strings in 2012.
en.identityCaveat: Applications ≠ awarded TLDs ≠ registry agreements ≠ TLD portfolio ≠ RSP-managed TLDs ≠ Internet governance. The numbers belong to different layers and must not be added together.
en.identity2026TopSub: After Reveal Day, this will be calculated from the official 2026 dataset. Legal applicants will be counted as published; a separate view may group applications by publicly disclosed direct / ultimate parent where the data supports it.
en.rootDistributedTitle: The root is coordinated through a small number of institutions, but served globally
en.rootDistributedBody: PTI manages root-zone changes and Verisign maintains the root-zone file, while 12 independent root-server operators serve 13 logical root identities through thousands of physical instances worldwide. Institutional coordination and physical delivery therefore have very different geographies.
en.geoInterpretBody: The dashboard can show where policy institutions, root functions, registry contracts, applicant headquarters and technical providers cluster. It cannot reduce Internet governance to headquarters, or equate a large TLD portfolio with control over ICANN policy or the DNS root.
en.contention2026Sub: Preliminary contention sets for identical applied-for strings will be available on Reveal Day. They may still change through replacement strings and later string-confusion procedures; 17 November will provide a clearer comparison point.
en.contentionCompareTitle: Competition is a cultural signal too
en.contentionCompareBody: The most contested strings show where many applicants independently saw the same future market. Comparing 2012 and 2026 turns contention from a procedural detail into a measure of changing expectations.

Neither measure is equivalent to control over ICANN policy.

en.driftIoReading: The registry itself now markets .io as “the domain for tech websites”, explicitly acknowledging the input/output reinterpretation and its place in startup culture.
en.driftAiReading: A geographic code became almost perfectly aligned with a later technology acronym; the registry now presents .AI as the “Domain of Artificial Intelligence”.
en.driftTvReading: The registry markets .TV around video and creator culture: the geographic code now communicates a media format to users worldwide.
en.driftMeReading: A country code became a pronoun and a personal-branding device. The registry explicitly describes .ME as globally personal rather than merely geographic.
en.driftCoReading: The shift was unusually explicit: IANA records early plans to commercialise .CO globally as a de-facto generic domain associated with “company”.
en.driftFmReading: The registry has deliberately positioned .FM as an industry-specific namespace for broadcasting, streaming, podcasting and social media.
en.driftReadingTitle: A namespace can be governed, but meaning also emerges from use.
en.driftReadingBody: A TLD has a formal status, but not necessarily a fixed cultural meaning. Registries define rules and eligibility; language, technology and communities can rewrite what people read after the dot. The same principle matters for .lugano: governance can define the perimeter, while actual use will shape what the namespace comes to mean.
en.downloadDriftSub: CSV · formal origin, acquired association and sources
en.odditiesTitle: When the DNS remembers a different world
en.odditiesSub: Country codes can outlive states, disappear with them, remain reserved, or describe places that barely behave like ordinary domain markets. The root is part directory, part institutional fossil record.
en.oddityReadingTitle: The root is not a clean map of today.
en.oddityReadingBody: The DNS inherits geography from standards, but transitions take time and historical exceptions survive. That makes the root a record of political change, administrative convention and technical continuity — not merely a list of current countries.
en.oddityGhostsSub: Some country-code domains survive political entities; others are deliberately retired after a transition.
en.oddityNeverTitle: A reused code that was not redelegated
en.oddityNeverSub: The history of a string and the history of the country code assigned to it can diverge.
en.oddityHistorySub: The United Kingdom is one of the clearest reminders that DNS history predates today’s tidy eligibility rules.
en.oddityTerritoriesSub: A territory can qualify for a ccTLD even when ordinary public registrations are absent or the place itself has no conventional population.
en.oddityBeyondTitle: Beyond the nation-state — and beyond Latin script
en.oddityBeyondSub: The ccTLD system can represent a supranational entity and the same identity in multiple writing systems.
en.oddSuFact: .SU was delegated in 1990 and IANA still marks it ACTIVE; IANA historical material identifies it as the Soviet Union code.
en.oddSuReading: A DNS label can outlive the state that originally gave it meaning.
en.oddYuFact: .YU was delegated for Yugoslavia in 1989 and removed from the root on 1 April 2010 after the transition to .RS and .ME.
en.oddYuReading: Retiring a ccTLD is a migration problem, not an instant edit to the map.
en.oddAnFact: .AN represented the Netherlands Antilles. After the territory dissolved in 2010, the code lost eligibility and the domain was retired while successor namespaces were introduced.
en.oddAnReading: Political fragmentation can require several successor namespaces rather than a one-for-one rename.
en.oddTpFact: .TP represented Portuguese Timor. After Timor-Leste became independent, .TL replaced it and .TP was removed from the root in 2015.
en.oddTpReading: A ccTLD can become a legacy dependency that must be wound down years after the political transition.
en.oddCsFact: .CS was formerly delegated for Czechoslovakia and later retired. ISO reassigned CS to Serbia and Montenegro in 2003, but .CS was not redelegated for that country, which continued using .YU until .RS and .ME were created.
en.oddCsReading: Reusing a country code does not automatically revive its former Internet delegation.
en.oddGbUkFact: ISO uses GB, yet the operational British ccTLD is .UK. IANA lists .GB as a reserved domain and treats .UK as a grandfathered historical exception.
en.oddGbUkReading: Internet naming history sometimes wins over later standardisation.
en.oddAqFact: .AQ is the ccTLD for Antarctica and has been delegated since 1992.
en.oddAqReading: The root can assign a geographic identity even to a continent without a normal nation-state or permanent population.
en.oddBvFact: .BV belongs to Bouvet Island. Norid says the TLD has never been opened for domain registrations.
en.oddBvReading: A TLD can exist technically without becoming a public namespace market.
en.oddSjFact: .SJ covers Svalbard and Jan Mayen. Norid says it has never been opened for registrations and points users toward .NO instead.
en.oddSjReading: Eligibility for a ccTLD does not imply that second-level registrations must be offered.
en.oddEuFact: .EU is treated as a country-code TLD even though the European Union is not a state; IANA recognises EU through an exceptionally reserved eligibility path.
en.oddEuReading: The country-code system contains institutional exceptions that do not map neatly onto sovereign states.
en.oddEuIdnFact: The European Union also has Cyrillic .ею and Greek .ευ forms, delegated through the IDN ccTLD process.
en.oddEuIdnReading: One political identity can exist at the top level in several scripts while remaining part of the same global root.
en.downloadOdditiesSub: CSV · geopolitical ghosts, historical exceptions and unusual ccTLDs
en.dotMapSub: A domain is a technical identifier with legal, economic, institutional and cultural dimensions. These eight perspectives explain what can gather around one name.
en.dotMapReadingTitle: The dot is technical. What societies build around it is not.
en.dotMapReadingBody: A useful way to read a TLD is to ask which layer is doing the work: addressing, allocation, governance, trust, market value, identity or cultural meaning.
en.dimAddressBody: A human-readable identifier that helps users and software find Internet resources.
en.dimContractBody: A registration exists through agreements among registrant, registrar and registry.
en.dimMarketBody: Names can carry retail prices, premium pricing, renewals and secondary-market value.
en.dimJurisdictionBody: Eligibility, policies and legal duties vary across namespaces and operators.
en.dimIdentityBody: A domain can accumulate reputation and become a persistent identifier for a person, place or institution.
en.dimTrustBody: Verification, DNSSEC and registry rules can add trust signals around a name.
en.dimCultureBody: Communities and language can give a TLD meanings that its original designation never anticipated.
en.dimPoliticsBody: Country codes, city names and allocation disputes can reflect institutions, borders and public authority.
en.domainRightTitle: What do you actually get when you register a domain?
en.domainRightSub: Registration is not the purchase of a piece of the Internet. A registrant enters a contractual relationship, and the name remains subject to renewal, registry policy and the applicable lifecycle.
en.lifeAvailableBody: The name is not currently registered and may be eligible under the registry policy.
en.lifeRegisteredBody: A registrant enters an agreement through a registrar and the registry records the name.
en.lifeRenewedBody: A registration can be renewed for another term; renewal is a possible loop, not a mandatory step before expiration.
en.lifeExpiredBody: If the registration term ends, post-expiration rules apply. Renewal or restoration may still be possible depending on policy and timing.
en.lifeRedemptionBody: If an applicable gTLD registration is deleted by the registrar, it enters a 30-day redemptionPeriod during which restoration may be possible.
en.lifeDeletedBody: After the lifecycle completes, a deleted name may become available for a new registration.
en.lifeCaveat: This is a simplified gTLD-oriented map, not one universal lifecycle. Expiration does not automatically equal deletion. Registry, registrar and ccTLD policies can differ.
en.economicsSub: The same domain can sit inside several markets at once: registration, renewal, premium pricing, registry services and secondary-market trading.
en.valueRegistrantBody: Chooses the name and pays the retail registration or renewal price.
en.valueRegistrarBody: Provides the retail channel and submits registration transactions to the registry.
en.valueRegistryBody: Operates the TLD database and sets the registry-side commercial and policy model within its framework.
en.valueIcannBody: For gTLDs, contractual and fee relationships also sit above the registry and registrar ecosystem.
en.valueAftermarketBody: Existing registrations can acquire resale value independently of the registry’s wholesale price.
en.economicsReading: A domain price is not one thing. Wholesale, retail, premium and aftermarket value belong to different layers.
en.controlLeversTitle: Who can actually pull which lever?
en.controlLeversSub: A website, a domain registration, DNS resolution and browser access are different layers. Different actors can intervene at different points; no single organization “controls the Internet”.
en.leverHostingBody: Can remove or disable content or infrastructure it hosts.
en.leverDnsBody: Can stop serving authoritative DNS or alter the zone it operates.
en.leverRegistrarBody: Maintains the registrant relationship and submits registration changes to the registry.
en.leverRegistryBody: Maintains the TLD registry and processes additions, changes or deletions under applicable rules.
en.leverBrowserBody: Can warn, block or distrust a destination without changing the registration itself.
en.leverIcannBody: Coordinates gTLD policy and contracts, but is not a general-purpose content regulator or Internet police force.
en.controlReadingBody: Taking content offline, suspending a registration, changing DNS and blocking access are not the same action. Governance starts by identifying the layer.
en.modelTitle: Two different questions: what kind of application is it, and who can register?
en.modelSub: ICANN application types and day-to-day registration access are different axes. A namespace can be geographic, community or brand-oriented and still impose very different access rules.
en.modelGeneralBody: An application that does not fall into a specialized application type.
en.modelCommunityBody: A specialized application linked to a clearly delineated community and the additional commitments required for that designation.
en.modelGeoBody: A specialized application for a string meeting the 2026 geographic-name criteria and applicable support or non-objection requirements.
en.modelBrandBody: A specialized application for an eligible string tied to a registered trademark and qualifying brand operator.
en.modelIdnBody: An application for a TLD string represented in a script supported through the Internationalized Domain Name framework.
en.modelGovBody: An application submitted by a government or intergovernmental organization and treated as specialized.
en.modelOpenBody: A namespace broadly open to eligible registrants under standard registry rules.
en.modelVerifiedBody: A namespace where eligibility must be verified; .BANK is an example for regulated banking organizations.
en.modelNote: These labels describe ICANN’s 2026 application designations. Historical TLDs are not presented here as if they were 2026 examples. “Open” or “restricted” instead describes practical registration access after delegation.
en.invisibleSub: The DNS already does much more than turn names into IP addresses. It routes mail, publishes authentication data and certificate-authorization policy, advertises services and can carry cryptographic trust.
en.dnsMailBody: MX records tell sending systems which mail servers handle email for a domain.
en.dnsAuthBody: SPF, DKIM and DMARC use DNS-published data to help receivers evaluate authorized and authenticated mail.
en.dnsCertBody: CAA records publish which certificate authorities are authorized to issue certificates for a domain.
en.dnsIntegrityBody: DNSSEC signs DNS data so resolvers can validate its origin and integrity through a chain of trust.
en.dnsDiscoveryBody: SRV records can advertise the hostname and port of services associated with a domain.
en.dnsHttpsBody: SVCB and HTTPS records can publish service endpoints and connection parameters before a client connects.
en.invisibleReading: The DNS is already an infrastructure layer for routing, discovery and trust. “Beyond the domain” is therefore an extension of existing capabilities, not a departure from what DNS already does.
en.scriptsTitle: The Internet is not written only in Latin characters
en.scriptsSub: Internationalized Domain Names allow top-level domains in non-ASCII scripts. Universal Acceptance is the practical requirement that browsers, email systems and applications actually accept them.
en.uaBody: A name can be valid in the global DNS and still fail in an application that assumes old ASCII-only or short-TLD rules. Universal Acceptance is about removing those technical barriers.
en.uaReading: Global naming requires more than delegation. Software has to recognize the names people are actually allowed to use.
en.universesSub: A dot-separated string can look like a domain while belonging to a different naming regime. Visual similarity does not mean the same root, resolver or governance system.
en.universePublicBody: .com, .ch, .中国 and other delegated TLDs live in the globally coordinated DNS root.
en.universeSpecialBody: .test, .localhost, .invalid, .onion and home.arpa have standards-defined special behavior; they are not ordinary public-root TLD registrations.
en.universeAlternativeBody: .eth is part of Ethereum Name Service; Handshake describes itself as an experimental peer-to-peer root naming system. These are different naming systems, not ICANN-root TLDs.
en.universeReadingTitle: Looks like a domain ≠ is a public DNS TLD.
en.universeReadingBody: The important question is not only what comes after the dot, but which root and resolution system gives that label meaning.
en.digitalResourceTitle: A country code can become a digital natural resource
en.digitalResourceSub: Semantic accidents can create real economic value. Anguilla’s .AI is the clearest current example: a two-letter country code became globally aligned with artificial intelligence.
en.aiRevenueLabel: 2026 Anguilla budget estimate · Domain Name Registration
en.aiRevenueCaveat: EC$253.6 million · budget estimate, not realized revenue
en.digitalResourceReadingBody: The economic value comes from a global meaning that the country did not invent but can govern and monetize. A ccTLD can therefore behave like a scarce national digital asset.
en.wordTitle: Who gets to control a word?
en.wordSub: Contention is only one version of scarcity. A second question is whether a generic word should ever become an exclusive namespace for one operator.
en.closedBody: ICANN defines a closed generic as a generic term proposed to be operated exclusively for the applicant’s own benefit. For the 2026 round, closed generic applications are not permitted unless and until an approved public-interest methodology exists.
en.closedExample: The issue is not “who won the auction?” but whether a generic word should be closed at all.
en.wordReadingTitle: Some strings are not merely brands. They are pieces of language.
en.wordReadingBody: When a namespace corresponds to a generic word, allocation can raise questions about competition, access and public interest that raw contention counts do not capture.
en.successSub: Registration volume is only one metric. A brand TLD, a verified community namespace and a civic TLD may have completely different purposes, so success has to be measured against mission.
en.successScaleBody: How many names are registered, and how quickly the namespace grows or contracts.
en.successUseBody: Whether names resolve to real services, websites, email or machine-readable endpoints.
en.successRenewalBody: Whether registrants keep names over time rather than treating the namespace as disposable inventory.
en.successTrustBody: Security controls, abuse rates, verification requirements and credibility attached to the namespace.
en.successDiversityBody: How registrations are distributed across registrants, registrars, sectors and geographies.
en.successPurposeBody: Whether the namespace achieves the mission for which it exists, even with modest raw volume.
en.successCivicBody: For civic namespaces: local adoption, verified actors, useful services, interoperability and measurable public value.
en.successReading: This is a framework, not a ranking. A TLD should be judged against the job it is meant to do.

en.lifePendingDeleteBody: If it is not restored during redemptionPeriod, the name enters pendingDelete for five days and cannot be restored.
en.lifeAvailableAgainBody: After purge from the registry database, the name may become available for registration again under the registry policy.
en.lifeDeletionPath: If the registrar deletes an applicable gTLD registration

en.modelVariantBody: An application involving variant strings evaluated together with the primary applied-for string.
en.modelSupportBody: An application from an applicant qualifying for assistance through the Applicant Support Program is treated as specialized.
en.controlSourceNote: ICANN states that it does not control Internet content and is not a general-purpose website takedown authority.

en.homeGuideLabel: START HERE · FIVE QUESTIONS TO GET ORIENTED
en.homeGuideTitle: A name. A history. Rules, money, people. A place in the world.
en.homeGuideIntro: A TLD is what comes after the last dot in a name, such as .com, .ch or .lugano. Behind that short ending are applications, rules, institutions, contracts, technology, money and communities. Start with the guided journey or choose a question.
en.homeWhoDecidesBody: ICANN, IANA, registries and registrars have different responsibilities. Knowing which actor can make which decision is the first step towards understanding the system.
en.homeWhoRunsBody: Rules, TLD operators and technical infrastructure are not all located in the same place. Seeing where they concentrate makes the system easier to understand.
en.homeWhatChangesBody: A proposed TLD name can also be a trademark, a region, a culture or a religious term. Objections, governments, auctions and review mechanisms can change what happens next.
en.homeScope: An independent research publication and structured archive. The Explorer connects IANA TLD records, ICANN applications, life histories and selected governance cases. Editorial interpretation is marked separately from sourced facts.
en.authorDisclosureBody: Robert Bregy is the municipal secretary of the City of Lugano and is involved in the .lugano project. This publication is a personal, independent research project. Its interpretations and scenarios do not constitute an official City position or decision.
en.publicQuestionsTitle: A vision to test against public evidence
en.publicQuestionsIntro: These are editorial questions for assessing a possible civic namespace. They describe neither adopted municipal targets nor services already delivered.
en.publicNeedBody: Which task would become easier or more reliable for a person, organization or service? A distinctive suffix alone does not demonstrate that benefit.
en.publicAdoptionBody: Do names lead to services people use? Published examples of active use would be stronger evidence than the number of names reserved or announced.
en.publicRulesBody: Can users understand who is eligible, who is responsible and how a problem can be reported? Confidence should rest on published rules and accountable practice.
en.publicOpenBody: Can people and software use the services through documented interfaces and accepted standards? Public documentation and working demonstrations would make this claim testable.
en.exploreRootListed: Present in the IANA root list
en.ianaRecordNote: Official fields from the preserved IANA record. An empty field means that IANA does not report it or it could not be reliably identified. The registry country is the country of the listed organization, not necessarily the place represented by the TLD. Personal contact details are available in the source.
en.ianaDatesNote: Registration, record update and retrieval are different dates. They do not establish when the present operator took over or which application round originated the TLD.
en.ianaReportsNote: Reports linked by IANA, with their original titles and publication dates. A report date is not necessarily the effective date of a delegation or transfer. The list is not a complete operator history.

en.updatesPolicy: Updates are published after source acquisition and checks. Source files and their hashes are preserved; historical events retain their own dates. The 2026 application layer is updated only from official publications, never automatically when a calendar date arrives.

en.journeyEyebrow: START HERE · NO TECHNICAL KNOWLEDGE NEEDED
en.journeyTitle: Behind a click: how the Internet works
en.journeyIntro: You typed a URL. Now follow what actually happens: the browser reads its parts, DNS finds an IP address, networks reach the server, HTTPS protects the connection, and the browser builds the page.
en.journeyFoundation: The Internet is a network of networks. Names such as example.com are convenient for people; networks forward data using IP addresses. DNS connects those two worlds. The Web then uses that network to exchange requests, responses and content.
en.journeyExample: An educational simulation, with no requests to the example website. 192.0.2.10 is reserved for documentation; it is not the real address of example.com.
en.journeyPhaseWeb: REACH THE SERVER AND RECEIVE THE PAGE
en.journeyNoJs: You can read all the steps below even without JavaScript.
en.journeyDnsLane: 01 · From the name to the destination
en.journeyDnsNote: If the answer is not already cached, the resolver follows delegations: the root points to .com, .com points to the DNS for example.com, and the authoritative DNS returns the requested data.
en.journeyWebLane: 02 · From the IP address to the page
en.journeyWebNote: From here, website traffic crosses networks and routers. The DNS servers have finished their job for this lookup.
en.journeyResolver: Resolver · finds where the name is
en.journeyTakeaway: The whole path: URL → name → DNS → IP → networks → HTTPS → request → page.
en.journeySimplified: This journey is simplified: caches and existing connections can skip some steps; others can overlap. A nearby server holding a copy may also deliver the page.
en.journeyAnatomy: See the parts of a domain
en.journeyHomeTitle: What happens when you open a website?
en.journeyHomeBody: From IP packets to domain names: a short simulation of what happens behind a click.
en.journey0Title: A URL tells the browser how, where and what to ask for
en.journey0Body: You typed https://www.example.com/news. https:// says how to communicate; www.example.com is the name to reach; /news is the requested resource. Before anything travels, the browser separates those jobs.
en.journey0Detail: A URL can also contain a port, query parameters and a fragment. We use a deliberately simple address here so the roles are visible without extra syntax.
en.journey1Title: The browser has to find www.example.com
en.journey1Body: People use readable names; the network needs to know which IP address should receive the data. The browser therefore relies on a DNS resolver to find where www.example.com can be reached.
en.journey1Detail: If a valid answer is already cached on the device or resolver, much of the DNS lookup can be skipped. The resolver may be supplied by your provider, organization or a service you choose.
en.journey2Body: If the answer is not already cached, the resolver can start at the DNS root. The root points to .com; the .com servers point to the DNS responsible for example.com. The final dot in www.example.com. represents the root and is normally omitted.
en.journey2Detail: The root and TLD mostly provide delegations: directions about where to ask next. They do not host the web page or carry its content. Running a TLD is a different role from hosting a website.
en.journey3Title: The name becomes an IP address
en.journey3Body: The authoritative DNS for example.com returns the requested data. The resolver gives it to your device. In this simulation: www.example.com → 192.0.2.10.
en.journey3Detail: Authoritative DNS servers publish data for the domains they serve. A records contain IPv4 addresses; AAAA records contain IPv6 addresses. One name can have several addresses, and several names can share an address.
en.journey4Title: Now the network knows where to send the packets
en.journey4Body: With the IP address available, packets can cross routers and networks until they reach the server. The Internet is not one network: it is a network of networks exchanging traffic.
en.journey4Detail: IP handles addressing and forwarding without guaranteeing delivery on its own. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 normally use TCP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. These transport choices sit above IP and help the exchange arrive reliably and efficiently.
en.journey5Title: The browser creates a protected connection
en.journey5Body: For HTTPS, the browser checks the certificate presented by the server for the requested name and establishes an encrypted connection. Data can now travel protected between browser and server.
en.journey5Detail: HTTPS protects communication and authenticates the server for that name. It does not certify that the operator is honest or the content is true. DNSSEC has a different job: verifying the origin and integrity of DNS data.
en.journey6Title: The browser asks for /news and builds what you see
en.journey6Body: Over the ready connection, the browser requests /news. The server responds with content and instructions; the browser interprets HTML, CSS, images and JavaScript and assembles the page.
en.journey6Detail: A visit may require more files, other servers and additional DNS lookups. A domain name and a website are separate things: you can move the content while keeping the same name and changing DNS.

en.guard5: Economic metrics retain their original accounting basis and currency. Public revenue, company revenue, operating income, transaction value, auction price and application fees are never treated as one comparable measure.
en.disputesIntro: A contention set means several applicants want the same or a confusingly similar string. A governance dispute is broader: governments, communities, rights holders or applicants can challenge who should operate a name, under what conditions, or whether it should exist at all.
en.disputesSelectionNote: These cases are selected because each exposes a different governance problem. They are not a league table and not a complete catalogue of every dispute in ICANN history.
en.disputesMechanismsTitle: How a TLD dispute can enter the system
en.disputesMechanismsSub: Not every fight is a lawsuit. The new-gTLD process has several formal routes for public-policy concerns, rights claims, community claims, competition and accountability review.
en.disputesCasesTitle: Nine disputes that changed what the dot means
en.disputesCasesSub: Each case separates the documented record from the question it raises about power, legitimacy and naming.
en.governanceCaseDrawerSub: This string is part of a selected dispute case in Connecting the Dots. The case narrative is editorial; the milestones and outcome are tied to cited primary sources.
en.mechanismGacBody: Governments can raise public-policy concerns through the Governmental Advisory Committee. Board treatment depends on the form of the advice and the applicable rules.
en.mechanismObjectionBody: Applications can face String Confusion, Legal Rights, Community or Limited Public Interest objections before independent dispute-resolution providers.
en.mechanismCpeBody: A qualifying community application in a contention set can seek priority by meeting the Applicant Guidebook criteria.
en.mechanismAuctionBody: When identical-string contention remains unresolved, an ICANN auction of last resort can determine which eligible applicant proceeds.
en.mechanismAccountabilityBody: Reconsideration and the Independent Review Process test whether ICANN followed its Bylaws, Articles and established procedures.
en.mechanismBoardBody: Some disputes ultimately require the Board to weigh application rules, GAC advice, accountability findings and the public interest.
en.caseXxxQuestion: Can ICANN reverse course on a controversial string, and what happens when its own accountability process disagrees?
en.caseXxxFact: .XXX moved from an unsuccessful 2000 proposal to the 2004 sponsored-TLD process. The Board later denied the application; ICM initiated the first IRP request heard by a panel, prevailed in 2010, and .XXX was delegated in 2011.
en.caseXxxReading: The case made ICANN accountability tangible: a politically sensitive string became a test of how far Board discretion can go and how that discretion can be reviewed.
en.caseXxxOutcome: .XXX was delegated in 2011 to ICM Registry LLC.
en.caseXxxEvent1: ICM proposed .xxx and .kids during the 2000 proof-of-concept round.
en.caseXxxEvent2: The Board authorized negotiations on commercial and technical terms for a .xxx registry agreement.
en.caseXxxEvent3: The Board denied the sponsored-TLD proposal.
en.caseXxxEvent4: ICM filed for Independent Review; the panel decided in ICM’s favor in 2010. It was the first IRP request heard by a panel.
en.caseAmazonQuestion: Who should be able to operate a TLD string that is also the name of a transnational region?
en.caseAmazonFact: Amazon applied for .AMAZON and two IDN equivalents in 2012. Brazil and Peru raised public-policy concerns, GAC consensus advice said the applications should not proceed, and the Board initially accepted that advice. Amazon later prevailed in an IRP; after further Board and government engagement, processing resumed and .AMAZON was delegated in 2020.
en.caseAmazonReading: The dispute exposed a fundamental collision between trademark-based corporate identity and geographic, cultural and governmental claims over the same word.
en.caseAmazonOutcome: .AMAZON was delegated in 2020 to Amazon Registry Services, Inc.
en.caseAmazonEvent1: Amazon submitted applications for .AMAZON and Chinese and Japanese IDN equivalents.
en.caseAmazonEvent2: GAC consensus advice said the applications should not proceed; the Board accepted that advice in 2014.
en.caseAmazonEvent3: Amazon challenged the decision through IRP and was declared the prevailing party in 2017; the panel recommended a fresh merits-based evaluation.
en.caseAmazonEvent4: After further negotiations and Board consideration, ICANN directed the applications to continue processing.
en.caseAfricaQuestion: How should a continent-name TLD be awarded when applicants disagree over legitimacy and government support?
en.caseAfricaFact: Two applicants sought .AFRICA. GAC consensus advice said DotConnectAfrica’s application should not proceed. DotConnectAfrica later prevailed on important process claims in an IRP, forcing ICANN to resume evaluation. The competing Registry.Africa application ultimately proceeded to delegation.
en.caseAfricaReading: The dispute became a landmark test of government advice, transparency and ICANN accountability in a geographically symbolic namespace.
en.caseAfricaOutcome: .AFRICA was delegated in 2017 to ZA Central Registry NPC trading as Registry.Africa.
en.caseAfricaEvent1: DotConnectAfrica Trust and ZA Central Registry applied for .AFRICA.
en.caseAfricaEvent2: GAC consensus advice said DotConnectAfrica’s application should not proceed, and ICANN halted its evaluation.
en.caseAfricaEvent3: An IRP panel found in favor of DotConnectAfrica on process-related claims and recommended that evaluation resume.
en.caseAfricaEvent4: The Board addressed the IRP outcome and the path toward delegation of the Registry.Africa application.
en.caseWebQuestion: Can funding and future-control arrangements behind an applicant change who is entitled to win a contention auction?
en.caseWebFact: Seven applicants sought .WEB. Nu Dot Co won the 2016 ICANN auction with a US$135 million bid. Verisign then disclosed that it had funded the bid under an arrangement contemplating future assignment of the registry agreement. Afilias challenged ICANN through a lengthy IRP. .WEB was finally delegated to Verisign in 2026.
en.caseWebReading: A simple contention set turned into a long argument about applicant identity, control, auction integrity and the boundary between financing and substitution.
en.caseWebOutcome: .WEB was delegated in July 2026 to VeriSign, Inc.
en.caseWebEvent1: Seven applicants entered the .WEB contention set.
en.caseWebEvent2: Nu Dot Co won ICANN’s auction of last resort with a US$135 million bid.
en.caseWebEvent3: Verisign disclosed that it had funded Nu Dot Co’s bid in exchange for, among other things, a contemplated future assignment of the .WEB registry agreement subject to ICANN consent.
en.caseWebEvent4: Afilias pursued an Independent Review Process challenging ICANN’s treatment of the arrangement and the auction outcome.
en.caseWebEvent5: .WEB entered the DNS root under VeriSign, Inc.
en.caseWineQuestion: How far should geographic-indication protections reach inside a global domain namespace?
en.caseWineFact: .WINE and .VIN triggered sustained government and producer concerns about names such as protected wine regions and appellations. The GAC had no consensus on additional safeguards. ICANN commissioned independent legal analysis and allowed the applications to proceed; both TLDs were delegated in 2015.
en.caseWineReading: The dispute showed that the DNS can become a venue for unresolved differences between trademark law, geographic indications and national trade-policy traditions.
en.caseWineEvent1: Applications for .WINE and .VIN entered the 2012 New gTLD Program.
en.caseWineEvent2: Governments and wine-sector organizations raised concerns over protection of geographic indications; the GAC did not reach consensus on extra safeguards.
en.caseWineEvent3: ICANN commissioned legal analysis and continued Board consideration of whether special protections were required.
en.casePatagoniaQuestion: What happens when a trademark is also the name of a geographic region shared by more than one country?
en.casePatagoniaFact: Patagonia, Inc. applied for .PATAGONIA. Argentina raised a GAC Early Warning and the application faced Community Objections, including from Argentina’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Independent Objector. The application was withdrawn.
en.casePatagoniaReading: Few cases explain the collision between brand identity and geographic identity more cleanly. The fact that a company owns a mark does not make every geographic meaning disappear.
en.casePatagoniaOutcome: The .PATAGONIA application was withdrawn and the string was not delegated.
en.casePatagoniaEvent1: Patagonia, Inc. applied for .PATAGONIA in the 2012 round.
en.casePatagoniaEvent2: The application received a GAC Early Warning and Community Objections connected to the geographic meaning of Patagonia.
en.caseIslamQuestion: Can a private applicant operate a globally sensitive religious term without broad support from the community it invokes?
en.caseIslamFact: Asia Green IT Systems applied for .ISLAM and .HALAL. GAC members raised sensitivities and concerns about community involvement and support, and the applications were held. The applicant later prevailed in an IRP on process issues, but after re-review the Board directed in 2018 that both applications not proceed.
en.caseIslamReading: The case tests a hard question the DNS cannot solve technically: who, if anyone, can legitimately speak for a global religious community in a top-level namespace?
en.caseIslamOutcome: .ISLAM and .HALAL did not proceed and were not delegated.
en.caseIslamEvent1: Asia Green IT Systems applied for .ISLAM and .HALAL.
en.caseIslamEvent2: GAC members and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation raised concerns; ICANN placed the applications on hold while those concerns were considered.
en.caseIslamEvent3: An IRP panel found the applicant to be the prevailing party on process claims, leading the Board to order a fresh review of the relevant advice and correspondence.
en.caseIslamEvent4: The Board directed that the .HALAL and .ISLAM applications not proceed.
en.caseMerckQuestion: What do “trademark rights” mean when different companies legitimately use the same historic name in different markets?
en.caseMerckFact: Merck KGaA and Merck Registry Holdings pursued overlapping MERCK-related strings and filed objections against one another’s applications. The dispute moved through objection, community-priority and accountability mechanisms. A .MERCK TLD was finally delegated in 2026 to Merck Registry Holdings, Inc.
en.caseMerckReading: The case breaks the comforting fiction that a famous brand name necessarily has one uncontested global owner. Domain governance has to operate across territorial trademark histories.
en.caseMerckOutcome: .MERCK was delegated in April 2026 to Merck Registry Holdings, Inc.
en.caseMerckEvent1: Merck-related applications entered the 2012 round from different corporate groups with overlapping naming claims.
en.caseMerckEvent2: The parties used Legal Rights, Community and related objection procedures against competing MERCK applications.
en.caseMerckEvent3: The dispute continued through Community Priority Evaluation and ICANN accountability proceedings.
en.caseMusicQuestion: Who gets to define a global “music community” strongly enough to receive priority for .MUSIC?
en.caseMusicFact: Eight applicants sought .MUSIC. Competing applicants and music-industry organizations used objections and Community Priority Evaluation, followed by reconsideration activity. DotMusic Limited ultimately signed a community Registry Agreement in 2021 and .MUSIC was delegated later that year.
en.caseMusicReading: The case shows that “community” is not a decorative label. In the new-gTLD process it can become a formal claim about representation, boundaries, support and enforceable registration policies.
en.caseMusicOutcome: .MUSIC was delegated in 2021 to DotMusic Limited under a community Registry Agreement.
en.caseMusicEvent1: Eight applications for .MUSIC entered the 2012 round.
en.caseMusicEvent2: Community Priority Evaluations considered competing claims to represent a defined music community.
en.caseMusicEvent3: The CPE process and related decisions were challenged through ICANN reconsideration and review activity.
en.caseMusicEvent4: DotMusic Limited signed the .MUSIC Registry Agreement and the TLD was delegated in 2021.
en.release0714: Disputed Dots: nine governance cases, Explorer cross-links and a rewritten site narrative connect applications and life histories to the disputes that shaped ICANN decision-making.
en.downloadGovernanceCasesSub: CSV · selected disputes, mechanisms and sources
en.homeWhoProfits: Who makes money from a dot?
en.homeWhoProfitsBody: A TLD can behave like national revenue, recurring infrastructure rent, a corporate asset, an auction prize or even a profitable withdrawal.
en.economicsCasesIntro: TLDs are naming infrastructure, but they can also create public revenue, recurring registry income, scarcity rents, acquisition value and financial barriers to entry. These cases keep unlike metrics separate rather than forcing them into one league table.
en.economicsSelectionNote: Selection rule: each case illustrates a distinct economic mechanism and is supported by attributable financial or institutional evidence. Revenue, valuation, auction price and public receipts are not interchangeable measures.
en.economicsModelsTitle: Eight ways money enters the namespace
en.economicsModelsSub: The same DNS root can generate very different economic relationships.
en.economicsCasesGridSub: Read each number in its own accounting context. The purpose is comparison of mechanisms, not a ranking of “most valuable TLDs”.
en.economicCaseDrawerSub: Documented financial evidence linked to this TLD. Different metric types are deliberately kept separate.
en.downloadEconomicCasesSub: CSV · economic mechanisms, strings and sources
en.downloadEconomicMetricsSub: CSV · values, currencies, accounting basis and sources
en.econModelSovereignRentBody: A country-code namespace becomes a material source of government revenue because global demand attaches value to its two-letter code.
en.econModelNationalContractBody: A state monetizes its ccTLD through a commercial registry or marketing agreement rather than operating a mass-market registrar business itself.
en.econModelOperatorAcquisitionBody: The company operating one or more namespaces is bought, turning expected registry cash flows into a transaction value.
en.econModelRecurringRegistryBody: Large installed bases and annual renewals can create highly recurring infrastructure revenue, but company-level results must not be mislabeled as revenue from one TLD.
en.econModelValuationRegulationBody: A registry contract can underpin billion-dollar valuation while price controls, public-interest duties and change-of-control review shape the asset.
en.econModelScarcityAuctionBody: When multiple applicants want the same string, scarcity can be converted into an auction price before the registry has sold a single domain.
en.econModelPrivateSettlementBody: Historical 2012-round mechanism: applicants could receive consideration for withdrawing from contention, so abandoning a string could generate accounting gains. Private contention resolution, including settlement agreements and compensation for withdrawal, is prohibited in the 2026 round.
en.econModelEntryBarrierBody: Application fees and additional evaluation costs determine who can afford to compete for a place in the root.
en.econAiQuestion: Can two letters become a national revenue asset?
en.econAiFact: Anguilla’s 2026 budget estimates EC$253.6 million from Domain Name Registration, up from EC$104.3 million actual in 2024.
en.econAiReading: The AI boom turned a legacy country code into something resembling a digital natural resource: global semantic demand generates public revenue for a small jurisdiction.
en.econTvQuestion: Can a country lease the commercial meaning of its country code?
en.econTvFact: Tuvalu’s 2024 budget allocated A$5.60 million to the Dot TV Marketing Agreement and projected A$5.87 million for 2026.
en.econTvReading: .tv shows a different sovereign model from .ai: value is captured through a commercial agreement tied to the global meaning of “TV”.
en.econIoQuestion: What is the operator of a fashionable ccTLD worth?
en.econIoFact: A secondary industry source reported that Afilias acquired Internet Computer Bureau, operator of .io, .ac and .sh, for US$70.17 million in cash in 2017.
en.econIoReading: The case shows that economic value can sit in the operating company and its registry cash flows, not in a simple notion that a TLD itself has a sale price.
en.econComQuestion: What does mature registry scale look like?
en.econComFact: Verisign reported US$1.66 billion of company revenue and US$1.12 billion of operating income in 2025; .com and .net ended the year with 173.5 million registrations combined.
en.econComReading: Recurring renewals, scale and high switching friction make mature registry infrastructure economically unlike a normal one-off domain sale. The figures are Verisign company results, not .com-only revenue.
en.econOrgQuestion: Can a registry contract underpin a billion-dollar valuation?
en.econOrgFact: The proposed 2019 acquisition of Public Interest Registry was publicly priced at US$1.135 billion, financed in part by a US$360 million term loan facility; ICANN ultimately withheld consent.
en.econOrgReading: .org exposes the tension between financial value and stewardship: an economically valuable recurring namespace can still be constrained by contractual approval, regulation and public-interest expectations.
en.econAuctionQuestion: How much will applicants pay for scarcity before launch?
en.econAuctionFact: ICANN last-resort auctions produced winning prices of US$135 million for .web, US$41.501 million for .shop and US$25.001 million for .app.
en.econAuctionReading: A string can acquire a nine-figure clearing price before operating revenue exists. The price reflects contention scarcity and strategic expectations, not an appraisal of the TLD as property.
en.econWithdrawalQuestion: Can losing or withdrawing be profitable?
en.econWithdrawalFact: Rightside reported a US$22.103 million net gain in 2014 and US$9.403 million in 2015 from withdrawals of interests in gTLD applications.
en.econWithdrawalReading: Private contention resolution created an unusual incentive: an application could have financial value even when the applicant never became registry operator.
en.econFeeQuestion: How expensive is the right to compete for the root?
en.econFeeFact: The base evaluation fee was US$185,000 in the 2012 round and is US$227,000 per application in the 2026 round, before certain additional fees or support discounts.
en.econFeeReading: The application fee is not a purchase price for a TLD. It is an entry cost into an uncertain evaluation process, and therefore part of the economic barrier to participation.
en.release0715: Economics of the Dot: economic cases, financial metrics, Explorer links and source-backed models added without conflating revenue, valuation, auctions or public receipts.
en.angle6: How country codes, renewals, auctions, acquisitions and application fees turn naming infrastructure into economic value.
en.homeWhoBelongsBody: Some TLDs express language, place, identity, community rules or social protection. A dot can be more than an address: it can become a claim of belonging.
en.socialCaseDrawerSub: Documented community rules and social purposes are shown as facts; the broader social meaning remains an editorial reading.
en.socialCasesTitle: The social life of the dot
en.socialCasesIntro: TLDs can mark language, territory, identity, professions, rights or community norms. These cases examine what a namespace asks of the people who use it and the community it claims to represent.
en.socialSelectionNote: This is a curated social reading, not a ranking of “social success”. Registration volume, community value and cultural significance are different things.
en.socialModelsTitle: Six ways a namespace becomes social
en.socialModelsSub: These categories describe different social functions and can overlap within the same TLD.
en.socialCasesGridSub: From linguistic communities to local nexus rules, safety policies and non-Latin scripts.
en.downloadSocialCasesSub: CSV · community, identity, inclusion and social-policy cases
en.socialModelLanguageBody: A namespace can give a language or cultural community a visible place in global naming.
en.socialModelCivicBody: A local nexus can turn a place name into a membership signal rather than generic branding.
en.socialModelIdentityBody: A string can become a flag for shared identity, values or representation.
en.socialModelInstitutionBody: Eligibility, verification and governance can bind a namespace to a defined community or institutional movement.
en.socialModelSafetyBody: Registry policies can try to create norms, protections or boundaries for vulnerable or sensitive communities.
en.socialModelScriptBody: Internationalized domain names remove the assumption that global naming must be written in Latin characters.
en.socialCatEligibility: Use Catalan online, promote Catalan culture, or address that community
en.socialCatGovernance: Community-based sponsored origin, now operated under an ICANN registry agreement
en.socialGalOrganization: PuntoGal is a non-profit organization rooted in Galician civil society
en.socialGalReinvestment: Profits are reinvested in promoting Galician language and culture
en.socialGalMemory: More than 7,000 .gal domains were collected for digital preservation in 2024
en.socialGayPurpose: A namespace explicitly framed around LGBTQ identity and a safer online space
en.socialGayDonation: The 2020 policies filed with ICANN committed 20% of registration revenue to recognized LGBTQ advocacy and activism charities
en.socialGayProtection: Additional measures targeted hate speech, cyberbullying and harassment
en.socialCoopEligibility: Restricted to cooperatives and eligible organizations supporting them
en.socialCoopVerification: Eligibility is verified and may be audited
en.socialNycNexus: Registrants must maintain a substantive lawful connection with New York City
en.socialNycConnection: The policy recognizes economic, cultural, historical, social or other lawful connections
en.socialKidsCommunity: A community application centered on children and child-related stakeholders
en.socialKidsProtection: The application framed .kids as a kids-friendly and kids-safe namespace
en.socialKidsDelegation: Delegated in 2022 to DotKids Foundation Limited
en.socialXxxSelfIdentification: The original sponsored model was based on voluntary self-identification by the adult-entertainment community
en.socialXxxPurpose: The charter included responsible practices, user choice and measures against illegal abusive material
en.socialXxxEvolution: The 2024 renewal moved from sponsorship to the Base Registry Agreement while carrying key commitments into PICs
en.socialIslamRepresentation: The applications sought to operate globally meaningful religious terms
en.socialIslamGovernment: GAC members and OIC states questioned community involvement, support and legitimacy
en.socialIdnScripts: Examples include Cyrillic, Arabic, Chinese and Devanagari top-level labels
en.socialIdnAccess: Users can navigate domain names in local languages and scripts instead of transliterating everything into Latin characters
en.socialIdnProcess: The IDN ccTLD Fast Track has enabled eligible countries and territories to request non-Latin country-name TLDs since 2009
en.socialCatQuestion: Can a TLD represent a language community rather than a state?
en.socialCatFact: The .cat charter says the namespace serves the Catalan Linguistic and Cultural Community. Eligibility includes using Catalan online, promoting Catalan culture or addressing that community.
en.socialCatReading: It separates cultural-linguistic belonging from state borders: a top-level domain can represent a community that is not reducible to one country.
en.socialGalQuestion: Can a namespace become part of a community’s cultural memory?
en.socialGalFact: PuntoGal is a non-profit organization that reinvests profits in Galician language and culture. In 2024, its official site reported that more than 7,000 .gal domains had been collected for preservation by national and regional libraries.
en.socialGalReading: The namespace functions not only as an identity marker but also as a corpus of digital life worth preserving.
en.socialGayQuestion: Can registry policy deliberately shape the social norms of a namespace?
en.socialGayFact: Policies filed with ICANN in 2020 committed 20% of registration revenue to recognized LGBTQ advocacy and activism charities and added measures against hate speech, cyberbullying and harassment.
en.socialGayReading: Here the registry is not neutral about social purpose: identity, redistribution and behavioral norms are built into the policy design.
en.socialCoopQuestion: What changes when a TLD verifies membership in a social and economic movement?
en.socialCoopFact: The .coop charter serves the international cooperative community. Current eligibility rules restrict registrations to cooperatives and qualifying support organizations and provide for verification.
en.socialCoopReading: The domain works as a membership signal: the string says something about the organizational model behind the registrant, not merely its website address.
en.socialNycQuestion: What does it mean to be “local” on a global network?
en.socialNycFact: The .nyc Nexus Policy requires registrants to maintain a substantive lawful connection with New York City and recognizes economic, cultural, historical, social and other lawful connections.
en.socialNycReading: The DNS becomes a boundary-making device: “New Yorker” is translated from a social idea into an eligibility rule.
en.socialKidsQuestion: Can a namespace make the Internet meaningfully safer for children?
en.socialKidsFact: DotKids Foundation applied for .kids as a community namespace centered on children and child-related stakeholders, framing it as kids-friendly and kids-safe. The TLD was delegated in 2022.
en.socialKidsReading: The case exposes the gap between labeling and protection: a trusted social meaning requires governance, enforcement and adoption, not merely a reassuring string.
en.socialXxxQuestion: Does putting sensitive content in a distinct namespace protect users, stigmatize a community, or both?
en.socialXxxFact: The original .xxx sponsored charter used voluntary self-identification by the adult-entertainment community and included goals around responsible practices and user choice. The 2024 renewal moved key commitments into Public Interest Commitments under the Base Registry Agreement.
en.socialXxxReading: A TLD can act like digital zoning. The social question is whether separation produces useful signaling and protection or simply relocates stigma into the namespace.
en.socialIslamQuestion: Who has the legitimacy to represent a global religious community in the DNS?
en.socialIslamFact: During the 2012 round, governments and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation challenged the .islam and .halal applications over community involvement, support and representational legitimacy. Neither string was delegated.
en.socialIslamReading: Some words are socially too large to behave like ordinary labels. The conflict was not only about technical competence but about who could credibly speak for a global community.
en.socialIdnQuestion: Who should have to transliterate their identity into someone else’s alphabet?
en.socialIdnFact: ICANN’s IDN framework supports domain names in local languages and scripts. Since 2009, the ccTLD Fast Track has enabled eligible countries and territories to request country-name TLDs in non-Latin scripts.
en.socialIdnReading: Internationalized TLDs turn script choice into an inclusion question: the global naming system becomes less dependent on Latin characters as the default doorway to the Internet.
en.guard6: Social significance is not inferred from registration volume. Registry charters, eligibility rules and documented community policies are FACT; the broader meaning assigned to them in this publication is a READING.
en.angle7: When does a TLD become a marker of language, locality, identity or belonging rather than simply an address?
en.release0716: The Social Life of the Dot: nine social cases, six social models, Explorer links and source-backed evidence on language, community, identity, safety and script inclusion.
en.release0717: Final audit hardening: corrected current ISO country codes in Explorer geography, aligned the publication snapshot to 4 October, clarified 2012 privacy handling and restored a self-checking release package.
en.release0718: Release integrity hardening: publication dates now derive from one state object; 2012 runtime enrichment no longer marks the full application corpus complete; archaeology counts are data-derived; 2026 round comparisons separate 1,663 submitted applications from 1,616 proceeding; historical private contention settlement is explicitly prohibited in 2026; release packaging, build metadata and QA are hardened.
en.heroPlain: A TLD is the ending of an Internet address, such as .com, .ch or .lugano. This site explains who can create one, who runs it and why it can matter.
en.release0719: Mobile journey hardening: the guided Internet walkthrough is now strictly viewport-bounded, puts the active explanation before its diagram on phones, reflows DNS and network diagrams on narrow screens, and keeps the current step in view when readers move forward or back.
en.release0720: Navigation clarity: the Italian menu now distinguishes “Stringhe contese” (competing applications for the same string) from “Controversie” (governance, legal or community disputes), removing an avoidable semantic ambiguity without changing the underlying sections or research data.
en.release0721: Automatic language entry: the root now respects an explicit saved language choice, otherwise detects the ordered browser language preferences, maps supported regional variants to EN / IT / DE / FR and falls back to English when no supported preference is available. Direct language URLs remain authoritative.
en.release0722: Guided-address focus: the sample URL now moves its visual emphasis with the walkthrough: the readable host name, the normally invisible DNS root dot, the TLD, the resolved IP, the network path, the HTTPS scheme and the requested page. The root dot appears only while it is being explained.
en.journeyTldAnswer: Points to the DNS for example.com
en.journeyAddressLane: An URL gives the browser three instructions
en.journeyUrlHowBody: Use the Web over a protected connection
en.journeyUrlWhereBody: Find this name and the server behind it
en.journeyNowLabel: What the Internet is doing now
en.journeyNow0To: the browser separates the URL into parts
en.journeyNow0Hint: How to communicate · which name to find · which resource to request.
en.journeyNow1Hint: The browser asks a DNS resolver where that name can be reached.
en.journeyNow2Hint: The DNS hierarchy moves from the root to the TLD and then to the authoritative DNS.
en.journeyNow3Hint: The resolver gives the device the address returned by the authoritative DNS.
en.journeyNow4Hint: Routers and networks forward packets toward the destination.
en.journeyNow5Hint: TLS authenticates the server for that name and protects data in transit.
en.journeyNow6Hint: The server responds; the browser interprets the files and builds what you see.
en.journey0Key: A URL is not just a website name: it contains different instructions for the browser.
en.journey1Key: Names are for people; IP addresses let networks reach destinations.
en.journey2Key: .com is not decoration: it is a real level in the DNS hierarchy.
en.journey3Key: DNS does not carry the page: it turns a name into information that helps locate the service.
en.journey4Key: The IP identifies the destination; routers decide hop by hop how to reach it.
en.journey5Key: HTTPS protects the transport and authenticates the server for that name; it does not guarantee that the content is true or trustworthy.
en.journey6Key: The page is the response to a request: the domain is the name used to reach the service, not the page itself.
en.journeyRecapTitle: From the URL to the page, at a glance
en.journeyRecapBody: These are conceptual stages, not a stopwatch: caches and existing connections can skip or overlap some of them. The chain is what matters.
en.release0723: Teaching-first Internet walkthrough: the seven steps now follow one coherent story from URL to name, DNS hierarchy, IP, networks, HTTPS and page. The DNS root is explained inside the hierarchy instead of as an isolated step; a live “what is happening now” strip, one key takeaway per step, sequential DNS delegation diagram and final recap make the relationship between URL anatomy, name resolution and web delivery explicit.
en.release0724: Navigation hardening: every user-initiated section change now lands at the start of the selected section on desktop and mobile; the brand is a real home link and reliably returns to the top of the overview. Internal anchored links, dynamically rendered Explorer cross-links, section indexes and the publication stamp share the same offset-aware navigation behavior.
